choices.why: It is a dozen words.

choices.text: Bigger chunks ignore headings
choices.why: Both sizes were embedded with the same path.

choices.text: Small chunks lose more when cut

prompt: A team embeds its chunks with one model and, to save money, embeds questions with a cheaper model of the same dimension. What happens?

choices.text: Scores look like similarities and mean nothing
choices.why: Right: two models, two spaces. The check refuses more than one model.

choices.text: It works, since the vectors have the same length
choices.why: Equal length does not make the spaces the same; the numbers mean different things.

choices.text: The database refuses the query
choices.why: pgvector compares any two vectors of the same dimension.

choices.text: Retrieval gets slightly worse but stays usable
choices.why: There is no partial meaning across two spaces.

prompt: Why does the table store path and text in separate columns when both go into the embedding?

choices.text: To keep the path out of the hash
choices.why: The hash covers path and text together.

choices.text: To print it once, as the source header
choices.why: Right, instead of repeating it inside every chunk's text.

choices.text: pgvector cannot store text longer than one line
choices.why: Text columns hold any length.

choices.text: The path changes every run
choices.why: It changes only when a heading does.

prompt: How many embedding requests did the first ingest.py run make for 137 chunks?
labembed refused the first request twice with 429. Why did ingest.py still embed all 137 chunks?

choices.text: ingest.py catches 429 and sleeps for one second
choices.why: ingest.py has no error handling of its own.

choices.text: The refused batch was skipped and embedded later
choices.why: Nothing was skipped; the same request succeeded on retry.

choices.text: labgen cached the vectors from the earlier run
choices.why: labgen passes embedding requests on; it caches nothing.

choices.text: The SDK retried by itself, within max_retries
choices.why: Right: three attempts, and the program never knew.

prompt: An overnight indexing run of two million chunks dies at batch 40,000 after exhausting its retries. With ingest.py's design, what is the cheapest recovery?
hint: What does a second run embed?

choices.text: Switch to a bigger batch size and rerun from zero
choices.why: From zero is the waste; batch size does not change it.

choices.text: Run it again
choices.why: Right: ids already in the table are kept, and only what is missing is sent. (As written, ingest.py commits at the end; a real run would commit per batch.)

choices.text: Lower the chunk size so there are fewer batches
choices.why: Smaller chunks mean more chunks, and new ids for all of them.

choices.text: Drop the table and start again with more retries
choices.why: That re-embeds the 40,000 batches already paid for.

choices.text: The heading path alone

choices.text: The position of the chunk in the document

prompt: After the refund sentence was edited, how many chunks did ingest.py embed?
Which change would leave every id the same and every vector wrong?
hint: The id says nothing about it.

choices.text: Switching to a different embedding model
choices.why: Right; the model column is there to make the switch deliberate.

choices.text: Editing a heading
choices.why: The path is in the hash, so the ids change.

choices.text: Adding a paragraph
choices.why: The chunks around it change text and get new ids.

choices.text: Deleting a document
choices.why: Its ids are removed; the rest are untouched and right.

prompt: A writer adds a long paragraph at the top of the shipping policy. Why might ingest.py re-embed several chunks, not one?

choices.text: The new paragraph exceeds 256 pieces
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with which ids change.

choices.text: Later chunks shift
choices.why: Right: chunks change text without anyone editing them.

choices.text: The hash covers the whole document
choices.why: It covers one chunk's path and text.

choices.text: Every edit re-embeds the whole document
choices.why: Only chunks whose text changed get new ids.

prompt: After marking a document superseded, why does a customer still see its chunks until lesson 14?

choices.text: ingest.py has not run yet
choices.why: It ran, and the status is in the table.

choices.text: The HNSW index caches the old status

choices.text: The search does not filter on status yet
choices.why: Right: the mark is data until a query uses it.

prompt: A colleague inserts a correction chunk into the table by hand, with no document behind it. What does the lesson say goes wrong?

choices.text: pgvector refuses rows without a doc_id

choices.text: No run of ingest.py would ever remove it

choices.text: The next run deletes it

choices.text: Its embedding comes from the wrong model

prompt: Why must the index be built with vector_cosine_ops?

choices.text: It matches the <=> operator
choices.why: Right: an index built for another operator is ignored, without an error.

choices.text: Cosine is the only distance HNSW supports
choices.why: HNSW supports L2, inner product and cosine.

choices.text: It is faster than the other operator classes
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; matching is.

choices.text: pgvector requires it for 384 dimensions
choices.why: Any operator class works for any dimension.

prompt: Why did the capture set enable_seqscan = off before EXPLAIN?

choices.text: Sequential scans give wrong results with vectors
choices.why: A sequential scan is exact; it is the index that is approximate.

choices.text: HNSW indexes are only used when it is off
choices.why: The planner uses them when they are cheaper.

choices.text: It makes the index build faster
choices.why: It affects query planning, not building.

choices.text: So EXPLAIN shows the index is usable
choices.why: Right: at 130 rows the planner prefers reading the table. It is not a setting to leave on.
